**Pierluigi Collina**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2) (born 13 February 1960) is an Italian former [football referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_(association_football) "Referee (association football)"). Widely regarded by pundits as one of the greatest referees of all time,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-6) he was named "The World's Best [Referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_(association_football) "Referee (association football)")" by the [International Federation of Football History & Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_Football_History_&_Statistics "International Federation of Football History & Statistics") a record six consecutive times from 1998 to 2003,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-7) and was named the best referee of all time by the same organisation, as well as by _[France Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France\_Football "France Football")_, in 2020.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-best_referee-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FranceFootball2020-9)

Collina is still involved in football as an unpaid consultant to the Italian Football Referees Association (AIA), the Head of Referees for the [Football Federation of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_Federation_of_Ukraine "Football Federation of Ukraine") since 2010,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-ColriU-10) a member of the [UEFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") Referees Committee, and Chairman of the FIFA referees committee.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-11)

## Refereeing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Refereeing career")]

Collina was born in [Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bologna "Bologna") and attended the [University of Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna "University of Bologna"), graduating with a degree in [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") in 1984.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12) During his teenage years, he played as a [centre-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre-back "Centre-back") for a local team, but was persuaded in 1977 to take a referee's course, where it was discovered that he had a particular aptitude for the job.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-TreccaniProfile2-13) Within three years he was officiating at the highest level of regional matches, while also completing his [compulsory military service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service#Italy "Military service").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-14) In 1988, he progressed more rapidly than normal to the national third division, [Serie C1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lega_Pro_Prima_Divisione "Lega Pro Prima Divisione") and [Serie C2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lega_Pro_Seconda_Divisione "Lega Pro Seconda Divisione").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-rivoluzionario-15) After three seasons, he was promoted to officiating [Serie B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serie_B "Serie B") and [Serie A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serie_A "Serie A") matches in 1991.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16)

Around this time, at the age of 26, Collina developed a severe form of [alopecia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopecia "Alopecia"), resulting in the permanent loss of all his facial hair, giving him his distinctive [bald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bald "Bald") appearance and earning the nickname _[Kojak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kojak "Kojak")_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-17) He later came to be known as the "Ice-cool Italian," or as the "[Iron Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man "Iron Man")," in the media, earning a reputation as a "strict" but "fair" referee, with a decisive and charismatic temperament, and self-control; he was often known for booking players who attempted to confront him. He soon came to be regarded as one of the best referees in Italy, and later, the world.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-TreccaniProfile2-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-Euro20001-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-19)

In 1995, he took charge of the second leg of the [Coppa Italia final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Coppa_Italia_final "1995 Coppa Italia final") between [Parma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parma_FC "Parma FC") and [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC"); this was the first of four Coppa Italia finals he officiated, with his other appearances occurring in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Coppa_Italia_final "2002 Coppa Italia final"), [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Coppa_Italia_final "2004 Coppa Italia final"), and [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Coppa_Italia_final "2005 Coppa Italia final").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16) That same year, after officiating at 43 Serie A matches, he was placed on [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA")'s International Referees List.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile3-20) He was allocated five matches at the [1996 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics"), including the final between [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria_national_football_team "Nigeria national football team") and [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-1996OlympicsF-21) He refereed the [1999 UEFA Champions League final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1999 UEFA Champions League final") between [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") and [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C."); he cited this as his most memorable game because of the cheers at the end, which he described as a "lions' roar".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-22)

[Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team") and England, and the round of 16 match between co-hosts [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_national_football_team "Japan national football team") and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_national_football_team "Turkey national football team");[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF1-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF2-31) in a tournament marked by several controversial refereeing decisions and errors, he was praised by pundits for his performance throughout the competition, in particular in the latter second round match.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-36) However, he also awarded a controversial decisive penalty in the aforementioned group match, for an alleged foul on [Michael Owen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Owen "Michael Owen") by [Mauricio Pochettino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauricio_Pochettino "Mauricio Pochettino"), which [David Beckham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") converted for the only goal of the game.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-42) In June 2002, Collina reached the pinnacle of his career, when he was chosen to officiate the [World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2002 FIFA World Cup final"), between [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team") and Germany.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF1-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF2-31) Prior to the game, Germany's [Oliver Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Kahn "Oliver Kahn") told the _[Irish Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Irish\_Times "The Irish Times")_: "Collina is a world-class referee, there's no doubt about that, but he doesn't bring luck, does he?" Kahn was referring to two previous high-profile matches that Collina had refereed which involved Kahn: the aforementioned [1999 UEFA Champions League final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1999 UEFA Champions League final"), a 2–1 defeat for Bayern; and Germany's [5–1 defeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_1-5_England_(2001) "Germany 1-5 England (2001)") against [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") in Munich in September 2001, in a [qualification match for the 2002 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA) "2002 FIFA World Cup qualification (UEFA)").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-43) Kahn's luck did not change in the final, and Germany lost 2–0 to the Brazilian side.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF-44)

Collina took charge of two consecutive [Supercoppa Italiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercoppa_Italiana "Supercoppa Italiana") finals in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Supercoppa_Italiana "2002 Supercoppa Italiana") and [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Supercoppa_Italiana "2003 Supercoppa Italiana"), his only two appearances in the competition.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16) He refereed the [2004 UEFA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Cup_final "2004 UEFA Cup final") between [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_CF "Valencia CF") and [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_de_Marseille "Olympique de Marseille"), sending off [Fabien Barthez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabien_Barthez "Fabien Barthez") in first-half stoppage time.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2004UCF1-23)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2004UCF2-45)[UEFA Euro 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2004 "UEFA Euro 2004") was his last major international tournament, as in February 2005, he reached the mandatory retirement age; he refereed the opening match between hosts [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_national_football_team "Portugal national football team") and eventual champions [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece_national_football_team "Greece national football team"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-46) as well as the semi-final between Greece and [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic_national_football_team "Czech Republic national football team"), his final international tournament match.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-47) His last international match was [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_national_football_team "Portugal national football team") against [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia_national_football_team "Slovakia national football team") on 4 June 2005, a [2006 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup")[qualifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA)#Group_3 "2006 FIFA World Cup qualification (UEFA)") at [Estádio da Luz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_da_Luz "Estádio da Luz") in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-48)

The [FIGC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Football_Federation "Italian Football Federation") raised its mandatory retirement age to 46 in order to accommodate Collina for a further season. However, a dispute emerged between the federation and Collina early in August 2005, following his decision to sign a sponsorship deal with [Opel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opel "Opel") (also advertising for [Vauxhall Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vauxhall_Motors "Vauxhall Motors") in the United Kingdom – both were owned by [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors") at the time). As Opel was also a sponsor of Serie A club [A.C. Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.C._Milan "A.C. Milan"), the deal was seen as a [conflict of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest") and Collina was not allowed to referee top-flight matches in Italy. In response, he handed in his resignation, effectively ending his career. The Italian Referees Association then attempted to reject his resignation, but Collina persisted with his retirement from the league.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-49)

Collina attracted the ire of [Luciano Moggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Moggi "Luciano Moggi"), the Juventus executive and chief instigator of the [2006 Italian football scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Italian_football_scandal "2006 Italian football scandal"). Collina was one of the referees that Moggi attempted to have punished for decisions that were made against Juventus. In an intercepted phone call, Moggi claimed that Collina and his colleague [Roberto Rosetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Rosetti "Roberto Rosetti") were too "objective" and should be "punished" for it.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-51) As a result, he and Rosetti were two of the few referees that emerged unscathed from the scandal.

After retiring from Serie A, Collina refereed the [Soccer Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer_Aid "Soccer Aid") matches for charity in May 2006 [[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-52) and September 2008. During the latter of these games, Collina was involved in an awkward fall and was stretchered off after 21 minutes of play.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-53) He later refereed the first half of the 2010 Soccer Aid match.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-54)

He came out of retirement to officiate a [third-round Champions League qualifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_UEFA_Champions_League_qualifying_rounds "2005–06 UEFA Champions League qualifying rounds") between [Everton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everton_F.C. "Everton F.C.") and [Villarreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villarreal_CF "Villarreal CF") on 24 August 2005 when he wrongly disallowed an Everton goal. He retired again soon after the game.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-55) In total, he officiated 240 matches in the Italian Serie A, 109 international matches, and 467 matches across all competitions throughout his career.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FranceFootball2020-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16)

## Later career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Later career")]

Collina served as the chief designator of the Italian Football Referees Association (AIA) for Serie A and Serie B from 2007 until 2010.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16)

Collina was appointed head of referees for the [Football Federation of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_Federation_of_Ukraine "Football Federation of Ukraine") since 2010.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-ColriU-10) His work in this position is criticised by national referees who disapprove of his lack of involvement in Ukrainian football (spending not more than two weeks per year in Ukraine) and possible tolerance towards corruption in the Ukrainian national football association.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-56)

Collina became the [UEFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") chief of referees in 2010. He held the role until he stepped down in 2018.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-57)

Collina became the chairman of the [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") referee committee in 2017. In this position, Collina most notably selects, evaluates, and appoints the referee crews for FIFA tournaments including the [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-58)

He was involved in the introduction and evaluation of the [video assistant referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_assistant_referee "Video assistant referee") system for the [2018 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_World_Cup "2018 World Cup"). During the tournament he pointed out the system's effectiveness[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-59) and later commented positively on its application.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-60)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Qatar_v_Japan_%E2%80%93_AFC_Asian_Cup_2019_final_06.jpg/250px-Qatar_v_Japan_%E2%80%93_AFC_Asian_Cup_2019_final_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Qatar_v_Japan_%E2%80%93_AFC_Asian_Cup_2019_final_06.jpg)

Collina during the [2019 AFC Asian Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_AFC_Asian_Cup_Final "2019 AFC Asian Cup Final") between [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_national_football_team "Japan national football team") and [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_national_football_team "Qatar national football team")

In 1988, Collina met his wife Gianna in [Versilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versilia "Versilia"). After living together almost from their meeting, they moved to the coastal town of [Viareggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viareggio "Viareggio"). Since their marriage, the couple have had two daughters.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-rivoluzionario-15) In 2003, Collina published his autobiography, _My Rules of the Game (Le Mie Regole del Gioco)_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-61) In August 2005, after his retirement, he concentrated on his own business, as a [financial advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_advisor "Financial advisor"). Today he lives in [Forte dei Marmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forte_dei_Marmi "Forte dei Marmi").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-62)

After refereeing the Second Round match between [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_national_football_team "Japan national football team") and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_national_football_team "Turkey national football team") at the [2002 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup "2002 FIFA World Cup"), Collina became famous in Japan, and appeared in a [television advert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_advertisement "Television advertisement") for [frozen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frozen_food "Frozen food")[takoyaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takoyaki "Takoyaki") products. He is also very popular in Turkey, as no Turkish team, national or club, lost a game with him in charge.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-63)

Although Collina is closely identified with football, his favourite sports club plays [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball"). He is a lifelong supporter of local club [Fortitudo Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortitudo_Bologna "Fortitudo Bologna").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-64) On 25 January 2010, Collina participated in a special match for supporting victims of the [earthquake in Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Haiti_earthquake "2010 Haiti earthquake") between a team called "Friends of [Zidane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinedine_Zidane "Zinedine Zidane") and [Ronaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronaldo_(Brazilian_footballer) "Ronaldo (Brazilian footballer)")" and [Benfica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.L._Benfica "S.L. Benfica") in Lisbon.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-66)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

### Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Music")]

In July 2002, he appeared in cartoon form in [George Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Michael "George Michael")'s video "[Shoot the Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_the_Dog "Shoot the Dog")".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-67)

### Advertising

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Advertising")]

In 2003, Collina appeared in an advert of a Turkish GSM operator, [Aria](https://tr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria%20(GSM%20operat%C3%B6r%C3%BC) "tr:Aria (GSM operatörü)"), due to his popularity in Turkey.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-68) In December 2004, he starred in a commercial for [MB Pivo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pivara_MB "Pivara MB") in Serbia, alongside [Lazar Ristovski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazar_Ristovski "Lazar Ristovski").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-69) His quote in Serbian "Nema cekaj Lazo, daj MB pivo" (I can't wait no longer Laza, give me MB beer) is famous in Serbia.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-70) He appeared in another MB Pivo advert two years later.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-71)

Collina's easily-recognisable face (to followers of football) also led to his appearance in an advertising campaign for the [Opel Vectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opel_Vectra "Opel Vectra") and [Signum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opel_Signum "Opel Signum") during the [2006 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-72) He also appeared in adverts for [MasterCard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MasterCard "MasterCard") and [Adidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas "Adidas") during the tournament.

### Video games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Video games")]

Collina was chosen as the cover figure for the football video games _[Pro Evolution Soccer 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro\_Evolution\_Soccer\_3 "Pro Evolution Soccer 3")_ and _[Pro Evolution Soccer 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro\_Evolution\_Soccer\_4 "Pro Evolution Soccer 4")_, appearing alongside compatriot [Francesco Totti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Totti "Francesco Totti") and [Thierry Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thierry_Henry "Thierry Henry") for the latter. This was unusual, as football games had come to almost exclusively feature only players and managers on their covers, and he did not feature in either game; this was the first time a referee had featured on the cover of a football video game.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-73) In addition, he featured as an "unlockable" referee in the rival [EA Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Sports "EA Sports") game _[FIFA Football 2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA\_Football\_2005 "FIFA Football 2005")_, released shortly before _Pro Evolution Soccer 4_.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-74)

**Pierluigi Collina**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2) (born 13 February 1960) is an Italian former [football referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_(association_football) "Referee (association football)"). Widely regarded by pundits as one of the greatest referees of all time,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-6) he was named "The World's Best [Referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_(association_football) "Referee (association football)")" by the [International Federation of Football History & Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_Football_History_&_Statistics "International Federation of Football History & Statistics") a record six consecutive times from 1998 to 2003,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-7) and was named the best referee of all time by the same organisation, as well as by _[France Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France\_Football "France Football")_, in 2020.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-best_referee-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FranceFootball2020-9)

Collina is still involved in football as an unpaid consultant to the Italian Football Referees Association (AIA), the Head of Referees for the [Football Federation of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_Federation_of_Ukraine "Football Federation of Ukraine") since 2010,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-ColriU-10) a member of the [UEFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") Referees Committee, and Chairman of the FIFA referees committee.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-11)

## Refereeing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Refereeing career")]

Collina was born in [Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bologna "Bologna") and attended the [University of Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna "University of Bologna"), graduating with a degree in [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") in 1984.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12) During his teenage years, he played as a [centre-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre-back "Centre-back") for a local team, but was persuaded in 1977 to take a referee's course, where it was discovered that he had a particular aptitude for the job.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-TreccaniProfile2-13) Within three years he was officiating at the highest level of regional matches, while also completing his [compulsory military service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service#Italy "Military service").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-14) In 1988, he progressed more rapidly than normal to the national third division, [Serie C1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lega_Pro_Prima_Divisione "Lega Pro Prima Divisione") and [Serie C2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lega_Pro_Seconda_Divisione "Lega Pro Seconda Divisione").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-rivoluzionario-15) After three seasons, he was promoted to officiating [Serie B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serie_B "Serie B") and [Serie A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serie_A "Serie A") matches in 1991.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16)

Around this time, at the age of 26, Collina developed a severe form of [alopecia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopecia "Alopecia"), resulting in the permanent loss of all his facial hair, giving him his distinctive [bald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bald "Bald") appearance and earning the nickname _[Kojak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kojak "Kojak")_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-17) He later came to be known as the "Ice-cool Italian," or as the "[Iron Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man "Iron Man")," in the media, earning a reputation as a "strict" but "fair" referee, with a decisive and charismatic temperament, and self-control; he was often known for booking players who attempted to confront him. He soon came to be regarded as one of the best referees in Italy, and later, the world.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-TreccaniProfile2-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-Euro20001-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-19)

In 1995, he took charge of the second leg of the [Coppa Italia final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Coppa_Italia_final "1995 Coppa Italia final") between [Parma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parma_FC "Parma FC") and [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC"); this was the first of four Coppa Italia finals he officiated, with his other appearances occurring in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Coppa_Italia_final "2002 Coppa Italia final"), [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Coppa_Italia_final "2004 Coppa Italia final"), and [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Coppa_Italia_final "2005 Coppa Italia final").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16) That same year, after officiating at 43 Serie A matches, he was placed on [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA")'s International Referees List.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile3-20) He was allocated five matches at the [1996 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics"), including the final between [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria_national_football_team "Nigeria national football team") and [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-1996OlympicsF-21) He refereed the [1999 UEFA Champions League final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1999 UEFA Champions League final") between [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") and [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C."); he cited this as his most memorable game because of the cheers at the end, which he described as a "lions' roar".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-22)

Collina served as a referee at the [1998 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_FIFA_World_Cup "1998 FIFA World Cup"); he took charge of two group matches: those between hosts [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team") and [Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark_national_football_team "Denmark national [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium_national_football_team "Belgium national football team").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2004UCF1-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-24) and the Group A match between [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") and defending champions [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_national_football_team "Germany national football team") (1–0),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-big_match-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-28) as well as the quarter-final between [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_national_football_team "Spain national football team") and eventual champions [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_national_football_team "France national football team") (1–2 with a [golden goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_goal_(association_football) "Golden goal (association football)")).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-29)

Collina also refereed at the 2002 FIFA World Cup,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2004UCF1-23) where he officiated the Group F match between [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team") and England, and the round of 16 match between co-hosts [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_national_football_team "Japan national football team") and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_national_football_team "Turkey national football team");[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF1-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF2-31) in a tournament marked by several controversial refereeing decisions and errors, he was praised by pundits for his performance throughout the competition, in particular in the latter second round match.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-36) However, he also awarded a controversial decisive penalty in the aforementioned group match, for an alleged foul on [Michael Owen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Owen "Michael Owen") by [Mauricio Pochettino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauricio_Pochettino "Mauricio Pochettino"), which [David Beckham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") converted for the only goal of the game.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-42) In June 2002, Collina reached the pinnacle of his career, when he was chosen to officiate the [World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup_final "2002 FIFA World Cup final"), between [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team") and Germany.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF1-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF2-31) Prior to the game, Germany's [Oliver Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Kahn "Oliver Kahn") told the _[Irish Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Irish\_Times "The Irish Times")_: "Collina is a world-class referee, there's no doubt about that, but he doesn't bring luck, does he?" Kahn was referring to two previous high-profile matches that Collina had refereed which involved Kahn: the aforementioned [1999 UEFA Champions League final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1999 UEFA Champions League final"), a 2–1 defeat for Bayern; and Germany's [5–1 defeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_1-5_England_(2001) "Germany 1-5 England (2001)") against [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") in Munich in September 2001, in a [qualification match for the 2002 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA) "2002 FIFA World Cup qualification (UEFA)").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-43) Kahn's luck did not change in the final, and Germany lost 2–0 to the Brazilian side.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2002FWCF-44)

Collina took charge of two consecutive [Supercoppa Italiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercoppa_Italiana "Supercoppa Italiana") finals in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Supercoppa_Italiana "2002 Supercoppa Italiana") and [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Supercoppa_Italiana "2003 Supercoppa Italiana"), his only two appearances in the competition.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16) He refereed the [2004 UEFA Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_UEFA_Cup_final "2004 UEFA Cup final") between [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_CF "Valencia CF") and [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_de_Marseille "Olympique de Marseille"), sending off [Fabien Barthez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabien_Barthez "Fabien Barthez") in first-half stoppage time.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2004UCF1-23)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-2004UCF2-45)[UEFA Euro 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2004 "UEFA Euro 2004") was his last major international tournament, as in February 2005, he reached the mandatory retirement age; he refereed the opening match between hosts [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_national_football_team "Portugal national football team") and eventual champions [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece_national_football_team "Greece national football team"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-46) as well as the semi-final between Greece and [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic_national_football_team "Czech Republic national football team"), his final international tournament match.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-47) His last international match was [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_national_football_team "Portugal national football team") against [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia_national_football_team "Slovakia national football team") on 4 June 2005, a [2006 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup")[qualifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA)#Group_3 "2006 FIFA World Cup qualification (UEFA)") at [Estádio da Luz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Est%C3%A1dio_da_Luz "Estádio da Luz") in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-48)

The [FIGC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Football_Federation "Italian Football Federation") raised its mandatory retirement age to 46 in order to accommodate Collina for a further season. However, a dispute emerged between the federation and Collina early in August 2005, following his decision to sign a sponsorship deal with [Opel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opel "Opel") (also advertising for [Vauxhall Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vauxhall_Motors "Vauxhall Motors") in the United Kingdom – both were owned by [General Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors "General Motors") at the time). As Opel was also a sponsor of Serie A club [A.C. Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A.C._Milan "A.C. Milan"), the deal was seen as a [conflict of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest") and Collina was not allowed to referee top-flight matches in Italy. In response, he handed in his resignation, effectively ending his career. The Italian Referees Association then attempted to reject his resignation, but Collina persisted with his retirement from the league.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-49)

Collina attracted the ire of [Luciano Moggi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Moggi "Luciano Moggi"), the Juventus executive and chief instigator of the [2006 Italian football scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Italian_football_scandal "2006 Italian football scandal"). Collina was one of the referees that Moggi attempted to have punished for decisions that were made against Juventus. In an intercepted phone call, Moggi claimed that Collina and his colleague [Roberto Rosetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Rosetti "Roberto Rosetti") were too "objective" and should be "punished" for it.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-51) As a result, he and Rosetti were two of the few referees that emerged unscathed from the scandal.

After retiring from Serie A, Collina refereed the [Soccer Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer_Aid "Soccer Aid") matches for charity in May 2006 [[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-52) and September 2008. During the latter of these games, Collina was involved in an awkward fall and was stretchered off after 21 minutes of play.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-53) He later refereed the first half of the 2010 Soccer Aid match.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-54)

He came out of retirement to officiate a [third-round Champions League qualifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005%E2%80%9306_UEFA_Champions_League_qualifying_rounds "2005–06 UEFA Champions League qualifying rounds") between [Everton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everton_F.C. "Everton F.C.") and [Villarreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villarreal_CF "Villarreal CF") on 24 August 2005 when he wrongly disallowed an Everton goal. He retired again soon after the game.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-55) In total, he officiated 240 matches in the Italian Serie A, 109 international matches, and 467 matches across all competitions throughout his career.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FranceFootball2020-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-treccaniProfile1-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16)

## Later career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Later career")]

Collina served as the chief designator of the Italian Football Referees Association (AIA) for Serie A and Serie B from 2007 until 2010.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-FIGCProfile-16)

Collina was appointed head of referees for the [Football Federation of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_Federation_of_Ukraine "Football Federation of Ukraine") since 2010.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-ColriU-10) His work in this position is criticised by national referees who disapprove of his lack of involvement in Ukrainian football (spending not more than two weeks per year in Ukraine) and possible tolerance towards corruption in the Ukrainian national football association.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-56)

Collina became the [UEFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA "UEFA") chief of referees in 2010. He held the role until he stepped down in 2018.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-57)

Collina became the chairman of the [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") referee committee in 2017. In this position, Collina most notably selects, evaluates, and appoints the referee crews for FIFA tournaments including the [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup "FIFA World Cup").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-58)

He was involved in the introduction and evaluation of the [video assistant referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_assistant_referee "Video assistant referee") system for the [2018 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_World_Cup "2018 World Cup"). During the tournament he pointed out the system's effectiveness[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-59) and later commented positively on its application.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-60)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Qatar_v_Japan_%E2%80%93_AFC_Asian_Cup_2019_final_06.jpg/250px-Qatar_v_Japan_%E2%80%93_AFC_Asian_Cup_2019_final_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Qatar_v_Japan_%E2%80%93_AFC_Asian_Cup_2019_final_06.jpg)

Collina during the [2019 AFC Asian Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_AFC_Asian_Cup_Final "2019 AFC Asian Cup Final") between [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_national_football_team "Japan national football team") and [Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_national_football_team "Qatar national football team")

In 1988, Collina met his wife Gianna in [Versilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versilia "Versilia"). After living together almost from their meeting, they moved to the coastal town of [Viareggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viareggio "Viareggio"). Since their marriage, the couple have had two daughters.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-rivoluzionario-15) In 2003, Collina published his autobiography, _My Rules of the Game (Le Mie Regole del Gioco)_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-61) In August 2005, after his retirement, he concentrated on his own business, as a [financial advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_advisor "Financial advisor"). Today he lives in [Forte dei Marmi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forte_dei_Marmi "Forte dei Marmi").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-62)

After refereeing the Second Round match between [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_national_football_team "Japan national football team") and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey_national_football_team "Turkey national football team") at the [2002 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FIFA_World_Cup "2002 FIFA World Cup"), Collina became famous in Japan, and appeared in a [television advert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_advertisement "Television advertisement") for [frozen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frozen_food "Frozen food")[takoyaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takoyaki "Takoyaki") products. He is also very popular in Turkey, as no Turkish team, national or club, lost a game with him in charge.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-63)

Although Collina is closely identified with football, his favourite sports club plays [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball"). He is a lifelong supporter of local club [Fortitudo Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortitudo_Bologna "Fortitudo Bologna").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-64) On 25 January 2010, Collina participated in a special match for supporting victims of the [earthquake in Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Haiti_earthquake "2010 Haiti earthquake") between a team called "Friends of [Zidane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zinedine_Zidane "Zinedine Zidane") and [Ronaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronaldo_(Brazilian_footballer) "Ronaldo (Brazilian footballer)")" and [Benfica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.L._Benfica "S.L. Benfica") in Lisbon.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-66)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

### Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Music")]

In July 2002, he appeared in cartoon form in [George Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Michael "George Michael")'s video "[Shoot the Dog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_the_Dog "Shoot the Dog")".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-67)

### Advertising

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Advertising")]

In 2003, Collina appeared in an advert of a Turkish GSM operator, [Aria](https://tr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria%20(GSM%20operat%C3%B6r%C3%BC) "tr:Aria (GSM operatörü)"), due to his popularity in Turkey.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-68) In December 2004, he starred in a commercial for [MB Pivo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pivara_MB "Pivara MB") in Serbia, alongside [Lazar Ristovski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazar_Ristovski "Lazar Ristovski").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-69) His quote in Serbian "Nema cekaj Lazo, daj MB pivo" (I can't wait no longer Laza, give me MB beer) is famous in Serbia.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-70) He appeared in another MB Pivo advert two years later.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-71)

Collina's easily-recognisable face (to followers of football) also led to his appearance in an advertising campaign for the [Opel Vectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opel_Vectra "Opel Vectra") and [Signum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opel_Signum "Opel Signum") during the [2006 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-72) He also appeared in adverts for [MasterCard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MasterCard "MasterCard") and [Adidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas "Adidas") during the tournament.

### Video games

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pierluigi_Collina&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Video games")]

Collina was chosen as the cover figure for the football video games _[Pro Evolution Soccer 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro\_Evolution\_Soccer\_3 "Pro Evolution Soccer 3")_ and _[Pro Evolution Soccer 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro\_Evolution\_Soccer\_4 "Pro Evolution Soccer 4")_, appearing alongside compatriot [Francesco Totti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Totti "Francesco Totti") and [Thierry Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thierry_Henry "Thierry Henry") for the latter. This was unusual, as football games had come to almost exclusively feature only players and managers on their covers, and he did not feature in either game; this was the first time a referee had featured on the cover of a football video game.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-73) In addition, he featured as an "unlockable" referee in the rival [EA Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EA_Sports "EA Sports") game _[FIFA Football 2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA\_Football\_2005 "FIFA Football 2005")_, released shortly before _Pro Evolution Soccer 4_.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierluigi_Collina#cite_note-74)

The **1996 UEFA Champions League final** was a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match played on 22 May 1996 between title holders [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Ajax "AFC Ajax") of the Netherlands and [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC") of Italy. The match ended in a 1–1 draw after extra time, forcing a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)"), which Juventus won 4–2.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-2) It was the club's second and most recent triumph in the competition. As of 2026, this is the last time a Dutch team appeared in a Champions League final.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The match was a repeat of the [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final") final, making it the fourth repeated final pairing.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-3) Ajax won the 1973 final 1–0. Ajax was defending the title, having won in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1995 UEFA Champions League final") when they defeated [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Milan "AC Milan") 1–0.

Juventus had not featured in the Champions League for nine years until this edition of the tournament. Juventus reached their fourth final. In the semi-finals, Juventus eliminated French side Nantes, with a 2-0 victory in the first leg at home, and 3–2 defeat in the return leg. Previously Juventus won the final in [1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_European_Cup_final "1985 European Cup final"), and lost in [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final") and [1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_European_Cup_final "1983 European Cup final").

Ajax reached their sixth final. In the semi-finals, Ajax eliminated Greek side Panathinaikos; they lost the first leg 1–0 at home, but won 3–0 in the second leg. Previously Ajax won the finals in [1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_European_Cup_final "1971 European Cup final"), [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_European_Cup_final "1972 European Cup final"), [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final") and [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1995 UEFA Champions League final"), and lost in [1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_European_Cup_final "1969 European Cup final").

Juventus entered the final as [1995–96 Serie A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_Serie_A "1995–96 Serie A") runners-up to Milan, as well as [1995 Supercoppa Italiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Supercoppa_Italiana "1995 Supercoppa Italiana") winners. Ajax entered the final as [1995–96 Eredivisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_Eredivisie "1995–96 Eredivisie") champions, [1995 Dutch Supercup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Dutch_Supercup "1995 Dutch Supercup") winners, [1995 UEFA Super Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UEFA_Super_Cup "1995 UEFA Super Cup") and [1995 Intercontinental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Intercontinental_Cup "1995 Intercontinental Cup") winners.

## Match

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Match")]

### Summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Summary")]

The start of the match was dominated by Juventus, while some of the young Ajax players committed various errors in this phase.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) In the 12th minute, Ajax defender [Frank de Boer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_de_Boer "Frank de Boer") clumsily headed the ball while falling back, allowing Juventus striker [Fabrizio Ravanelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_Ravanelli "Fabrizio Ravanelli") to quickly get between de Boer and goalkeeper [Edwin van der Sar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_van_der_Sar "Edwin van der Sar"), who was coming out of his net, and despite the very angled position, slid in the net to give Juventus the lead.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4)

Ajax responded well, pushing further towards Juventus' half, taking advantage of their physical strength.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-CIHEFE-5) From a corner kick, [Nwankwo Kanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nwankwo_Kanu "Nwankwo Kanu") forced the Juventus goalkeeper [Angelo Peruzzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelo_Peruzzi "Angelo Peruzzi") to make a tough save,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) only for Ajax to later get a free kick in the 41st minute that surprised Peruzzi[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-6) who only managed to block the ball which fell at the feet of [Jari Litmanen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jari_Litmanen "Jari Litmanen") to tap in to equalise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) Just before half-time, [Antonio Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Conte "Antonio Conte") was subbed out due to injury, replaced with [Vladimir Jugović](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Jugovi%C4%87 "Vladimir Jugović").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-7)

The two teams went into half-time at 1–1, a score that remained unchanged in the second half where the only clear chance was for Juventus captain [Gianluca Vialli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluca_Vialli "Gianluca Vialli"), who from a very good position shot just wide of the net,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) as well as a miss from [Angelo Di Livio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelo_Di_Livio "Angelo Di Livio").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-CIHEFE-5)

After extra-time, the match remained 1–1 and went to penalty shoot-out.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) The only clear chance in the extra-time was an opportunity missed by Juventus player [Alessandro Del Piero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Del_Piero "Alessandro Del Piero") in the second half.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-CIHEFE-5) In the penalty shoot-out, all four Juventus penalty takers scored, with those being [Ciro Ferrara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciro_Ferrara "Ciro Ferrara"), [Gianluca Pessotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluca_Pessotto "Gianluca Pessotto"), [Michele Padovano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michele_Padovano "Michele Padovano") and Jugović. For Ajax, [Edgar Davids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Davids "Edgar Davids") the first penalty taker's shot was saved by Peruzzi. The next two players scored, those being Litmanen and [Arnold Scholten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Scholten "Arnold Scholten"). Their final penalty taken by [Sonny Silooy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Silooy "Sonny Silooy") was also saved. Jugović's goal was the decisive penalty that gave Juventus its second title in the competition; Juventus won by a score of 4–2.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4)

## Post-match

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-match")]

Although Juventus won the 1996 Champions League final, the victory remains controversial because of accusations of [doping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_sport "Doping in sport").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-9) The Juventus team has been accused of using [erythropoietin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin") (EPO) and the matter went to trial in 2004.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-10) In November 2004, club doctor Riccardo Agricola was given a 22-month prison sentence and fined €2,000 for sporting fraud by providing performance-enhancing drugs, specifically EPO, to players between 1994 and 1998,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-12) Leading hematologist Giuseppe d'Onofrio said that it was "practically certain" that midfielders [Antonio Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Conte "Antonio Conte") and [Alessio Tacchinardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessio_Tacchinardi "Alessio Tacchinardi") had taken EPO to overcome brief bouts of [anemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anemia "Anemia"), and that it was "very probable" that seven other players – [Alessandro Birindelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Birindelli "Alessandro Birindelli"), [Alessandro Del Piero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Del_Piero "Alessandro Del Piero"), [Didier Deschamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Deschamps "Didier Deschamps"), [Dimas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimas_(footballer) "Dimas (footballer)"), [Paolo Montero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Montero "Paolo Montero"), [Gianluca Pessotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluca_Pessotto "Gianluca Pessotto") and [Moreno Torricelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moreno_Torricelli "Moreno Torricelli") – had taken EPO in small doses.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-13)

In April 2005, the [Court of Arbitration for Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Arbitration_for_Sport "Court of Arbitration for Sport") gave the following advisory opinion, in part: "The use of pharmaceutical substances which are not expressly prohibited by sports law, and which cannot be considered as substances similar or related to those expressly prohibited, is not to be sanctioned by disciplinary measures. However, regardless of the existence or not of any judgement rendered by a State court, sports authorities are under the obligation to prosecute the use of pharmaceutical substances which are prohibited by sports law or any other anti-doping rule violation in order to adopt disciplinary measures."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-14) In December 2005, Agricola was acquitted of the charges by Turin's court of appeal.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-15) In March 2007, in the final verdict by the [Supreme Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Cassation_(Italy) "Supreme Court of Cassation (Italy)"), stated that "in the years of 1994 to 1998 there was no ascertained positive case of doping substances by Juventus players, that the purchase of erythropoietin or its administration to the athletes of the club does not emerge from any act of the trial, and that the same expert had identified the possibility of an administration of erythropoietin in distant terms from the sure evidence ("very probable" and in two cases "practically certain"): it is that therefore, the judgement of probability and not of certainty, did not allow for a statement of responsibility."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Cassation-16) The verdict also went on to say: "In response to the conclusion taken, the territorial court notes that there were no deferred values higher than the limits set in the various antidoping protocols and that the situation of the Juventus players, both with reference to the average hematological values, and in relation to that of material balance, did not differ from the national average population.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Cassation-16)

The **1996 UEFA Champions League final** was a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match played on 22 May 1996 between title holders [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Ajax "AFC Ajax") of the Netherlands and [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC") of Italy. The match ended in a 1–1 draw after extra time, forcing a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)"), which Juventus won 4–2.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-2) It was the club's second and most recent triumph in the competition. As of 2026, this is the last time a Dutch team appeared in a Champions League final.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The match was a repeat of the [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final") final, making it the fourth repeated final pairing.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-3) Ajax won the 1973 final 1–0. Ajax was defending the title, having won in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1995 UEFA Champions League final") when they defeated [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Milan "AC Milan") 1–0.

Juventus had not featured in the Champions League for nine years until this edition of the tournament. Juventus reached their fourth final. In the semi-finals, Juventus eliminated French side Nantes, with a 2-0 victory in the first leg at home, and 3–2 defeat in the return leg. Previously Juventus won the final in [1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_European_Cup_final "1985 European Cup final"), and lost in [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final") and [1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_European_Cup_final "1983 European Cup final").

Ajax reached their sixth final. In the semi-finals, Ajax eliminated Greek side Panathinaikos; they lost the first leg 1–0 at home, but won 3–0 in the second leg. Previously Ajax won the finals in [1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_European_Cup_final "1971 European Cup final"), [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_European_Cup_final "1972 European Cup final"), [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final") and [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UEFA_Champions_League_final "1995 UEFA Champions League final"), and lost in [1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_European_Cup_final "1969 European Cup final").

Juventus entered the final as [1995–96 Serie A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_Serie_A "1995–96 Serie A") runners-up to Milan, as well as [1995 Supercoppa Italiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Supercoppa_Italiana "1995 Supercoppa Italiana") winners. Ajax entered the final as [1995–96 Eredivisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_Eredivisie "1995–96 Eredivisie") champions, [1995 Dutch Supercup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Dutch_Supercup "1995 Dutch Supercup") winners, [1995 UEFA Super Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UEFA_Super_Cup "1995 UEFA Super Cup") and [1995 Intercontinental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Intercontinental_Cup "1995 Intercontinental Cup") winners.

## Match

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Match")]

### Summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Summary")]

The start of the match was dominated by Juventus, while some of the young Ajax players committed various errors in this phase.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) In the 12th minute, Ajax defender [Frank de Boer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_de_Boer "Frank de Boer") clumsily headed the ball while falling back, allowing Juventus striker [Fabrizio Ravanelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_Ravanelli "Fabrizio Ravanelli") to quickly get between de Boer and goalkeeper [Edwin van der Sar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_van_der_Sar "Edwin van der Sar"), who was coming out of his net, and despite the very angled position, slid in the net to give Juventus the lead.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4)

Ajax responded well, pushing further towards Juventus' half, taking advantage of their physical strength.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-CIHEFE-5) From a corner kick, [Nwankwo Kanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nwankwo_Kanu "Nwankwo Kanu") forced the Juventus goalkeeper [Angelo Peruzzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelo_Peruzzi "Angelo Peruzzi") to make a tough save,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) only for Ajax to later get a free kick in the 41st minute that surprised Peruzzi[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-6) who only managed to block the ball which fell at the feet of [Jari Litmanen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jari_Litmanen "Jari Litmanen") to tap in to equalise.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) Just before half-time, [Antonio Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Conte "Antonio Conte") was subbed out due to injury, replaced with [Vladimir Jugović](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Jugovi%C4%87 "Vladimir Jugović").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-7)

The two teams went into half-time at 1–1, a score that remained unchanged in the second half where the only clear chance was for Juventus captain [Gianluca Vialli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluca_Vialli "Gianluca Vialli"), who from a very good position shot just wide of the net,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) as well as a miss from [Angelo Di Livio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelo_Di_Livio "Angelo Di Livio").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-CIHEFE-5)

After extra-time, the match remained 1–1 and went to penalty shoot-out.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4) The only clear chance in the extra-time was an opportunity missed by Juventus player [Alessandro Del Piero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Del_Piero "Alessandro Del Piero") in the second half.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-CIHEFE-5) In the penalty shoot-out, all four Juventus penalty takers scored, with those being [Ciro Ferrara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciro_Ferrara "Ciro Ferrara"), [Gianluca Pessotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluca_Pessotto "Gianluca Pessotto"), [Michele Padovano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michele_Padovano "Michele Padovano") and Jugović. For Ajax, [Edgar Davids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Davids "Edgar Davids") the first penalty taker's shot was saved by Peruzzi. The next two players scored, those being Litmanen and [Arnold Scholten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Scholten "Arnold Scholten"). Their final penalty taken by [Sonny Silooy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Silooy "Sonny Silooy") was also saved. Jugović's goal was the decisive penalty that gave Juventus its second title in the competition; Juventus won by a score of 4–2.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-UEFA-4)

## Post-match

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-match")]

Although Juventus won the 1996 Champions League final, the victory remains controversial because of accusations of [doping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_sport "Doping in sport").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-9) The Juventus team has been accused of using [erythropoietin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin") (EPO) and the matter went to trial in 2004.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-10) In November 2004, club doctor Riccardo Agricola was given a 22-month prison sentence and fined €2,000 for sporting fraud by providing performance-enhancing drugs, specifically EPO, to players between 1994 and 1998,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-12) Leading hematologist Giuseppe d'Onofrio said that it was "practically certain" that midfielders [Antonio Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Conte "Antonio Conte") and [Alessio Tacchinardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessio_Tacchinardi "Alessio Tacchinardi") had taken EPO to overcome brief bouts of [anemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anemia "Anemia"), and that it was "very probable" that seven other players – [Alessandro Birindelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Birindelli "Alessandro Birindelli"), [Alessandro Del Piero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Del_Piero "Alessandro Del Piero"), [Didier Deschamps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didier_Deschamps "Didier Deschamps"), [Dimas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimas_(footballer) "Dimas (footballer)"), [Paolo Montero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Montero "Paolo Montero"), [Gianluca Pessotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianluca_Pessotto "Gianluca Pessotto") and [Moreno Torricelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moreno_Torricelli "Moreno Torricelli") – had taken EPO in small doses.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-13)

In April 2005, the [Court of Arbitration for Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Arbitration_for_Sport "Court of Arbitration for Sport") gave the following advisory opinion, in part: "The use of pharmaceutical substances which are not expressly prohibited by sports law, and which cannot be considered as substances similar or related to those expressly prohibited, is not to be sanctioned by disciplinary measures. However, regardless of the existence or not of any judgement rendered by a State court, sports authorities are under the obligation to prosecute the use of pharmaceutical substances which are prohibited by sports law or any other anti-doping rule violation in order to adopt disciplinary measures."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-14) In December 2005, Agricola was acquitted of the charges by Turin's court of appeal.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-15) In March 2007, in the final verdict by the [Supreme Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Cassation_(Italy) "Supreme Court of Cassation (Italy)"), stated that "in the years of 1994 to 1998 there was no ascertained positive case of doping substances by Juventus players, that the purchase of erythropoietin or its administration to the athletes of the club does not emerge from any act of the trial, and that the same expert had identified the possibility of an administration of erythropoietin in distant terms from the sure evidence ("very probable" and in two cases "practically certain"): it is that therefore, the judgement of probability and not of certainty, did not allow for a statement of responsibility."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Cassation-16) The verdict also went on to say: "In response to the conclusion taken, the territorial court notes that there were no deferred values higher than the limits set in the various antidoping protocols and that the situation of the Juventus players, both with reference to the average hematological values, and in relation to that of material balance, did not differ from the national average population.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Cassation-16)
