The **1999 UEFA Champions League final** was an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match between [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") of England and [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") of Germany, played at [Camp Nou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou") in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Spain, on 26 May 1999, to determine the winner of the [1998–99 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_UEFA_Champions_League "1998–99 UEFA Champions League"). [Injury time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football#Duration_and_tie-breaking_methods "Association football") goals from Manchester United's [Teddy Sheringham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Sheringham "Teddy Sheringham") and [Ole Gunnar Solskjær](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ole_Gunnar_Solskj%C3%A6r "Ole Gunnar Solskjær") cancelled out [Mario Basler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Basler "Mario Basler")'s early goal for Bayern to give Manchester United a 2–1 win and their first European Cup title since [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_European_Cup_final "1968 European Cup final"), their second overall. Referee Pierluigi Collina has cited this match as one of the most memorable of his career, and described the noise from the crowd at the end of the game as being like a "lion's roar".

The two sides had played each other earlier in the competition, having both been drawn in Group D in the group stage; Bayern won the group, while Manchester United qualified for the knockout phase as one of the two best runners-up across all six groups. After beating [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan") in the quarter-finals, Manchester United beat another Italian side, [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC"), in the semis to reach the final; meanwhile, Bayern beat fellow Germans [1. FC Kaiserslautern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Kaiserslautern "1. FC Kaiserslautern") in the quarter-finals, before overcoming Ukrainian side [Dynamo Kyiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Dynamo_Kyiv "FC Dynamo Kyiv") in the semis. The victory completed a [treble-winning season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_Manchester_United_F.C._season "1998–99 Manchester United F.C. season") for Manchester United, having already secured the [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_FA_Premier_League "1998–99 FA Premier League") and [FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_FA_Cup "1998–99 FA Cup") titles in the preceding 10 days. Bayern were also playing for a treble, having won the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_Bundesliga "1998–99 Bundesliga") and reached the [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_DFB-Pokal "1998–99 DFB-Pokal") final, although they went on to lose [that match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_DFB-Pokal_Final "1999 DFB-Pokal Final") as well to [Werder Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SV_Werder_Bremen "SV Werder Bremen") on penalties. It has been widely regarded as one of the greatest finals in the history of the tournament.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") and [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") had only met twice in competitive matches before the final, both meetings coming earlier in the 1998–99 season and both finished as draws.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-head_to_head-2) Manchester United's only other German opponents in their history were [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"), against whom they had an overall winning record, with three wins, two defeats and a draw in their six matches, including a 10–1 aggregate win in the second round of the [1964–65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964%E2%80%9365_Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup "1964–65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup") and a 2–0 aggregate defeat in the [1996–97 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996%E2%80%9397_UEFA_Champions_League "1996–97 UEFA Champions League") semi-finals.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-3) Bayern Munich had an equally narrow advantage in their 22 matches against English opposition, with seven wins, nine draws and six defeats, including a win over [Leeds United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_United_F.C. "Leeds United F.C.") in the [1975 European Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_European_Cup_final "1975 European Cup final") and a defeat to [Aston Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_F.C. "Aston Villa F.C.") in the [1982 final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_European_Cup_final "1982 European Cup final").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-4)

Including the victory over Leeds in 1975, Bayern Munich had won the European Cup on three occasions going into the 1999 final. With three victories in a row from [1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_European_Cup_final "1974 European Cup final") to [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_European_Cup_final "1976 European Cup final"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-5) they became only the third team to achieve such a feat after [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF") ([1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_European_Cup_final "1956 European Cup final") to [1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_European_Cup_final "1960 European Cup final"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-6) and [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Ajax "AFC Ajax") ([1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_European_Cup_final "1971 European Cup final") to [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final")).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-7) They had also finished as runners-up twice: in 1982 against Aston Villa[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-8) and [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final") against [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Porto "FC Porto").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-9) Although Bayern had been waiting 23 years for a European Cup title, Manchester United had had to wait even longer, as their only victory had come in [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_European_Cup_final "1968 European Cup final") against [Benfica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.L._Benfica "S.L. Benfica") at Wembley in extra time.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-10) Their manager then was [Matt Busby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Busby "Matt Busby"), who had been seriously injured 10 years earlier in the [Munich air disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_air_disaster "Munich air disaster"), which killed eight of his players on the way back from a European Cup tie in Belgrade, before rebuilding the team to become European Cup winners. Busby died in 1994; the day of the 1999 Champions League final would have been his 90th birthday.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-treble_joy-11)

Although it was the second Champions League season to feature clubs that had not won their national leagues the year before, Manchester United and Bayern Munich were the first such clubs to reach the final of the competition.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):354 Nevertheless, both went into the match as champions, having won their domestic leagues in 1998–99; Bayern Munich claimed the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga") title with a 1–1 draw against [Hertha BSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertha_BSC "Hertha BSC") on 9 May with three games to go, while Manchester United left it until the last day of the season (16 May), when they came back from 1–0 down against [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C.") to win 2–1 and beat [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_F.C. "Arsenal F.C.") to the title by a point.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-13) Both teams were also playing for the [treble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treble_(association_football) "Treble (association football)"); in addition to their league win, Manchester United had beaten [Newcastle United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_F.C. "Newcastle United F.C.") in the [1999 FA Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FA_Cup_Final "1999 FA Cup Final") on 22 May to claim the [Double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_(association_football) "Double (association football)"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-14) while Bayern were due to play [Werder Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SV_Werder_Bremen "SV Werder Bremen") in the [1999 DFB-Pokal Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_DFB-Pokal "1998–99 DFB-Pokal") on 12 June.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-sky_treble-15)

### Qualifying round

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Qualifying round")]

Since neither Manchester United nor Bayern Munich had won their respective leagues in 1997–98, both sides faced a qualifier to enter the 1998–99 Champions League. Manchester United were drawn against Polish champions [ŁKS Łódź](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81KS_%C5%81%C3%B3d%C5%BA "ŁKS Łódź") and won 2–0 on aggregate, goals from [Ryan Giggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Giggs "Ryan Giggs") and [Andy Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Cole "Andy Cole") in the first leg at [Old Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Trafford "Old Trafford") giving them the victory.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-17) Bayern Munich had an easier time against Yugoslavian champions [Obilić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK_Obili%C4%87 "FK Obilić"), winning 4–0 in the first leg at the [Olympiastadion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiastadion_(Munich) "Olympiastadion (Munich)") with goals from [Stefan Effenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Effenberg "Stefan Effenberg"), [Giovane Élber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovane_%C3%89lber "Giovane Élber"), [Alexander Zickler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zickler "Alexander Zickler") and [Thorsten Fink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorsten_Fink "Thorsten Fink"), all scored in the space of 17 second-half minutes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-18) In the second leg, played at [Partizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK_Partizan "FK Partizan")'s ground in Belgrade, an 88th-minute goal from [Lothar Matthäus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothar_Matth%C3%A4us "Lothar Matthäus") rescued a 1–1 draw to give Bayern a 5–1 win on aggregate.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-19)

### Group stage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Group stage")]

In the draw for the group stage, Bayern Munich were placed in Pot 2 and Manchester United in Pot 3 as Germany was higher than England in the UEFA association club coefficient rankings. They were drawn together in Group D, along with Spanish champions [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") and Danish champions [Brøndby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%B8ndby_IF "Brøndby IF"), in what became known as the "group of death".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-20) United and Bayern found themselves bottom of the group after the first round of matches, in which Bayern lost 2–1 away to Brøndby after surrendering a 1–0 lead in the last three minutes;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-21) United, meanwhile, played out a 3–3 draw at home to Barcelona after twice giving up the lead.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-22) The first group stage meeting between United and Bayern took place at the Olympiastadion on matchday 2 and finished in a 2–2 draw; Élber opened the scoring for Bayern before goals from [Dwight Yorke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Yorke "Dwight Yorke") and [Paul Scholes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Scholes "Paul Scholes") gave United the lead, only for a [Teddy Sheringham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Sheringham "Teddy Sheringham") own goal – brought about by an error by [Peter Schmeichel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schmeichel "Peter Schmeichel") – to level the scores in the 89th minute.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-23)

Matchdays 3 and 4 saw double-headers, with Manchester United taking on Brøndby and Bayern Munich playing Barcelona. Manchester United beat Brøndby 6–2 in their first match at [Parken Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parken_Stadium "Parken Stadium") in Copenhagen,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-24) then 5–0 at Old Trafford two weeks later.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-25) Bayern also recorded a pair of victories over Barcelona, winning 1–0 at the Olympiastadion[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-26) and 2–1 at the Camp Nou.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-27) On matchday 5, United played their second match against Barcelona – their first trip of the season to the Camp Nou – and again the two sides played out a 3–3 draw.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-28) With Bayern beating Brøndby 2–0 at home, the German side moved onto 10 points and took top spot in the group going into the final round of matches, one point ahead of United.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-29) Qualification for the quarter-finals was only guaranteed for the group winners,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-30) meaning that both United and Bayern had to play for victory in their final match against each other at Old Trafford. United took the lead just before half-time through a [Roy Keane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Keane "Roy Keane") strike from just outside the penalty area; however, [Hasan Salihamidžić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasan_Salihamid%C5%BEi%C4%87 "Hasan Salihamidžić") equalised for Bayern in the 55th minute and the game finished as a 1–1 draw. The result meant that Bayern finished as group winners, but United's 10 points from their six matches was enough to see them go through as one of the two group runners-up with the best record.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-33)

### Knockout stage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Knockout stage")]

In the quarter-finals, Bayern Munich were drawn against Group F winners and fellow German side [1. FC Kaiserslautern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Kaiserslautern "1. FC Kaiserslautern"), while Manchester United were paired with Group C winners [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan"). Two Yorke goals gave United a 2–0 win in their first leg at Old Trafford,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-34) while Bayern beat Kaiserslautern by the same scoreline at the Olympiastadion through goals from Élber and Effenberg.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-35) In the second leg, [Nicola Ventola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Ventola "Nicola Ventola") pulled a goal back for Inter, but Paul Scholes secured United's passage to the semi-finals with a late away goal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-36) Meanwhile, Bayern won convincingly at Kaiserslautern, as goals from Effenberg, [Carsten Jancker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carsten_Jancker "Carsten Jancker"), [Mario Basler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Basler "Mario Basler") and an own goal from [Uwe Rösler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uwe_R%C3%B6sler "Uwe Rösler") gave them a 4–0 win, 6–0 on aggregate.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-37)

United again came up against Italian opposition in the semi-finals, facing [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC"), who had beaten Greek side [Olympiacos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiacos_F.C. "Olympiacos F.C.") in the quarters, and Bayern were drawn against Ukrainian side [Dynamo Kyiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Dynamo_Kyiv "FC Dynamo Kyiv"), who beat reigning champions Real Madrid to reach the semis. Both first legs finished as draws; Giggs scored in injury time to secure a 1–1 home draw for Manchester United after [Antonio Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Conte "Antonio Conte") had put Juventus ahead midway through the first half,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-38) while Bayern also had to come from behind to draw 3–3 in Kyiv.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-39) A single goal from Basler proved the difference between Bayern and Dynamo in the second leg, giving the Germans a 4–3 aggregate win.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-40) Manchester United fell behind early in the [second leg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC_2%E2%80%933_Manchester_United_F.C. "Juventus FC 2–3 Manchester United F.C.") in Turin, as [Filippo Inzaghi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Inzaghi "Filippo Inzaghi") scored twice in the first 11 minutes. Goals from Keane and Yorke before half-time levelled the tie but gave United the advantage on away goals, before Cole secured victory with the winning goal seven minutes from the end of the match.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-41)

## Pre-match

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pre-match")]

### Venue and ticketing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Venue and ticketing")]

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Camp_Nou_aerial_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Camp_Nou_aerial_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Camp_Nou_aerial_(cropped).jpg)

The capacity of the [Camp Nou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou") stadium was reduced from over 100,000 to 92,000 for the final.

The [Camp Nou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou") stadium in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Spain, was selected as the venue for the final at a meeting of the UEFA Executive Committee in Lisbon, Portugal, on 6 October 1998.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-42) The selection process had begun more than four months earlier, in May 1998, when FC Barcelona submitted the Camp Nou as a contender to host the match in recognition of the club's centenary year.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-43) The other venues in contention to host the match were London's [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)") and Marseille's [Stade Vélodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_V%C3%A9lodrome "Stade Vélodrome"), but the Camp Nou was considered by UEFA's Stadiums Commission to be the favourite for its superior security, comfort and capacity.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-44) The Camp Nou had hosted one previous European Cup final: Italian club [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Milan "AC Milan")'s 4–0 victory over [Steaua București](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FCSB "FCSB") of Romania in [1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_European_Cup_final "1989 European Cup final"). It had also hosted two [Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup "UEFA Cup Winners' Cup") finals, in [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final "1972 European Cup Winners' Cup Final") and [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final "1982 European Cup Winners' Cup Final"); the latter was won on home turf by Barcelona.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-45)

The Camp Nou was constructed over three years from 1954 to 1957 as a replacement for Barcelona's previous home, the nearby [Camp de Les Corts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_de_Les_Corts "Camp de Les Corts").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-camp_nou_history-46) The original capacity of the Camp Nou was just over 93,000,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-camp_nou_history-46) but its first major European final, the 1972 Cup Winners' Cup Final, was attended by just 35,000 spectators.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-47) 1982 was the stadium's busiest year to date, hosting not only the 1982 Cup Winners' Cup Final, but also five matches at the [FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_FIFA_World_Cup "1982 FIFA World Cup"), including the opening match, all three matches in Group A of the second group stage and the semi-final between [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland_national_football_team "Poland national football team") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team"). Subsequent renovations meant that by 1999, the stadium's capacity had reached 115,000.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-camp_nou_history-46)

Due to UEFA regulations regarding standing at football matches, the Camp Nou's terraced sections were closed for the 1999 Champions League final, reducing the capacity to approximately 92,000. Of these, around two-thirds were reserved for the two finalist clubs (approximately 30,000 tickets each). The remaining third was divided between fans of FC Barcelona (around 7,500 tickets), UEFA, and competition sponsors.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):339 After an initial announcement that the clubs would only receive 25,000 tickets each, the [Independent Manchester United Supporters Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Manchester_United_Supporters_Association "Independent Manchester United Supporters Association") (IMUSA) called that figure "ridiculous", claiming it would push black market prices to "astronomical levels"; the group's spokesman, Lee Hodgkiss, suggested a figure closer to 50,000 would be more appropriate, given the stadium's usual capacity of around 115,000.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-48) Despite the club receiving only 30,000 tickets, it was estimated that up to 100,000 Manchester United fans travelled to Barcelona for the final, paying around £300 for flights and around £1,000 for match tickets.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):346 Many were able to buy tickets from touts, who had paid up to £400 to buy from Barcelona fans who had bought through their club for the equivalent of £28.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):339–340

As well as reducing the capacity of the stadium, UEFA also mandated that the Camp Nou pitch be narrowed by 4 metres (13 ft) from 72 metres (236 ft) to 68 metres (223 ft), to match UEFA's 'standard' pitch size.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):327

### Match officials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Match officials")]

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Pierluigi_Collina_2010.jpg/250px-Pierluigi_Collina_2010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pierluigi_Collina_2010.jpg)

Pierluigi Collina was the referee for the match.

The match referee was Pierluigi Collina of the [Italian Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Football_Federation "Italian Football Federation"). Collina was promoted to the FIFA International Referees list in 1995, and took charge of his first UEFA Cup matches in the [1995–96 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_UEFA_Cup "1995–96 UEFA Cup"). He had only refereed eight Champions League matches before the 1999 final, three of which came in the group stage earlier in the season, including the match between Barcelona and Bayern Munich at the Camp Nou on 4 November 1998; however, he had also taken charge of four matches at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_tournament "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament"), including the final between [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria_national_under-23_football_team "Nigeria national under-23 football team") and [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_under-23_football_team "Argentina national under-23 football team"), and two group stage matches at the [1998 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_FIFA_World_Cup "1998 FIFA World Cup").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-49) Collina was supported by fellow Italian officials Gennaro Mazzei and [Claudio Puglisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Puglisi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Claudio Puglisi (page does not exist)") as assistant referees, and fourth official Fiorenzo Treossi.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-officials-50)

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Nike_NK_800_Geo_1999_Champions_League_Final.JPG/250px-Nike_NK_800_Geo_1999_Champions_League_Final.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nike_NK_800_Geo_1999_Champions_League_Final.JPG)

The match ball for the final was the Nike NK 800 Geo, a white ball with a standard 32-panel design. It featured a large "[swoosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swoosh "Swoosh")" across two adjacent hexagonal panels with the Champions League logo on a pentagonal panel above, and a pattern of five-pointed stars similar to those used in the UEFA Champions League logo over the entire surface of the ball.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-51)

### Kits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Kits")]

As both Manchester United and Bayern Munich's primary kits featured significant amounts of red, UEFA regulations about kit clashes would normally have required both teams to wear their change kits. However, the two clubs felt it would have been a shame for neither to wear their traditional colours, and they agreed to toss a coin to see who would have first choice. Manchester United won the toss and therefore wore their usual European colours of red shirts, white shorts and white socks, while Bayern wore silver shirts, shorts and socks, all with maroon trim.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):360

### Opening ceremony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Opening ceremony")]

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_opening_ceremony.jpg/250px-1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_opening_ceremony.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_opening_ceremony.jpg)

The opening ceremony featured inflatable versions of recognisable Barcelona landmarks.

Before kick-off, opera singer [Montserrat Caballé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montserrat_Caball%C3%A9 "Montserrat Caballé") – moving around the field on the back of a golf cart[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-52) – performed a live version of "[Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_(Freddie_Mercury_and_Montserrat_Caball%C3%A9_song) "Barcelona (Freddie Mercury and Montserrat Caballé song)")", a song she recorded with the late [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)") lead singer [Freddie Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury "Freddie Mercury") in 1987, accompanied by a recording of Mercury on the stadium's electronic screen.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-53) The opening ceremony featured inflatable versions of some of Barcelona's most recognisable landmarks,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-leith_132-54) as well as flag-bearers waving flags of the crests of the participating teams. Bayern Munich's fans, meanwhile, created a [tifo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tifo "Tifo") of the name of their team with thousands of coloured cards.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-leith_132-54)

Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Kahn "Oliver Kahn") wore the armband for Bayern.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-aizelwood-62) As Manchester United's top two goalscorers throughout the season, Cole and Yorke started up front, leaving Sheringham—who had played a part in both goals in the FA Cup Final a few days earlier—on the bench. Also on the bench were fellow striker [Ole Gunnar Solskjær](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ole_Gunnar_Solskj%C3%A6r "Ole Gunnar Solskjær"), back-up goalkeeper [Raimond van der Gouw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raimond_van_der_Gouw "Raimond van der Gouw"), defenders [David May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_May_(footballer) "David May (footballer)"), [Phil Neville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Neville "Phil Neville") and [Wes Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Brown "Wes Brown"), and midfielder [Jonathan Greening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Greening "Jonathan Greening").

Bayern coach [Ottmar Hitzfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottmar_Hitzfeld "Ottmar Hitzfeld") announced his team's line-up for the final two full days ahead of the match.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bayern_lineup-63) Injuries also impacted on his selections, with French left-back [Bixente Lizarazu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bixente_Lizarazu "Bixente Lizarazu") and Brazilian forward Élber having suffered season-ending knee injuries.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-65) Élber's absence resulted in Bayern playing a three-man attack of Basler, Jancker and Zickler, while Lizarazu was replaced on the left flank by [Michael Tarnat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Tarnat "Michael Tarnat") playing in a wing-back role opposite [Markus Babbel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus_Babbel "Markus Babbel") on the right.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-66) Babbel was originally intended to play a man-marking role on Giggs, with his defensive abilities earning him selection ahead of the more attack-minded [Thomas Strunz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Strunz "Thomas Strunz");[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-bayern_lineup-63) however, this was nullified by Giggs' selection on the right wing, where he would play against Tarnat. The Bayern defence was anchored around sweeper Matthäus, who played behind [Thomas Linke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Linke "Thomas Linke") and Ghana international [Samuel Kuffour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Kuffour "Samuel Kuffour") – the only non-German in the Bayern side (by comparison, Manchester United had four Englishmen in their team); Linke and Kuffour's partnership at centre-back meant club captain [Thomas Helmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Helmer "Thomas Helmer") had to settle for a place on the bench.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-aizelwood-62) Effenberg and [Jens Jeremies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jens_Jeremies "Jens Jeremies") played in central midfield for Bayern, with Jeremies man-marking Beckham.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-67)

### Summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Summary")]

#### First half

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: First half")]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_teams_line_up.jpg/250px-1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_teams_line_up.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_teams_line_up.jpg)

The teams line up ahead of kick-off.

Six minutes into the match, Johnsen fouled Bayern striker Jancker just outside the area,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) and Basler placed a low free kick around the United wall to score the first goal, as Schmeichel was caught flat-footed.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) Although they were now a goal down, United began to dominate possession, but failed to create any clear-cut chances. The Bayern defence remained strong and well-organised, as Cole found out when his close-range effort was quickly closed down by three defenders.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) As Bayern began to look increasingly dangerous on the counter-attack than their opponents did in possession, Jancker repeatedly tested the United back four with a number of clever runs, some of which were flagged offside.

Cole once again found himself with a chance in the Bayern box, but goalkeeper Kahn hurried out of his goal to punch the ball to safety. At the other end, Basler came close with another free kick before Zickler sent a shot just wide from the edge of the box. As half-time approached, United winger Giggs, playing out of position on the right, sent a weak header towards Kahn from a Cole cross, but that was as close as they were to come to a goal in the first half.

#### Second half

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Second half")]

The German team started the second half in a more positive mood, with Jancker forcing a save from Schmeichel within a minute after the restart.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) Basler was proving to be Bayern's most dangerous player, first firing a 30-yard shot towards goal and then setting up a header for Babbel, who missed the ball entirely. United put together an attack when, after a healthy period of possession, Giggs crossed towards Blomqvist, who could only knock the ball over the bar after a desperate stretch.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) Another chance for Basler prompted Ferguson to bring on Sheringham for Blomqvist which resulted in a return to the more common formation of Giggs on the left (having started right-wing), with Beckham moving from an uncommon central to his more familiar right midfield position. Yorke dropped further back into a central midfield position.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) Hitzfeld responded with a substitution of his own, bringing on [Mehmet Scholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmet_Scholl "Mehmet Scholl"), who immediately set up Effenberg for a long-range shot that went narrowly wide. Schmeichel kept his side in the game when tipping another Effenberg shot over the bar after 75 minutes.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-wheeler-69) Scholl then almost scored from a delicate 20-yard chip after a run from Basler, but the ball bounced back off the post and into Schmeichel's arms.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) With the game seemingly drifting away from the English side, Ferguson introduced Solskjær to replace Cole with 10 minutes remaining.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-wheeler-69) The substitute immediately forced Kahn into a diving save with a header; it was the closest United had come to scoring all game.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) A minute later, Bayern missed a chance to secure the trophy, when an [overhead kick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_kick "Bicycle kick") from Jancker came off the crossbar.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-key_moments-68) As the game crept into the last five minutes, United's two substitutes forced Kahn into more saves, firstly through a Sheringham volley and then from another Solskjær header.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-70)

##### Injury time

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Injury time")]

> Beckham, in towards Schmeichel. It's come for Dwight Yorke. Cleared... Giggs with the shot, _Sheringham!_ Name on the trophy! Teddy Sheringham, with 30 seconds of added time played, has equalised for Manchester United – they are _still_ in the European Cup!

—[Clive Tyldesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Tyldesley "Clive Tyldesley") on [ITV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_(TV_network) "ITV (TV network)")'s broadcast call of Sheringham's injury time equaliser[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-The_Commentator's_Tale-71)

United won a corner when Effenberg deflected Gary Neville's cross over the Bayern goal line just as the [fourth official](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_referee_(association_football)#Fourth_official "Assistant referee (association football)") indicated three minutes of injury time. With so little time left for an equaliser, Schmeichel ventured up to Bayern's [penalty area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_area "Penalty area"). Beckham flighted the corner in just over Schmeichel's head, Yorke put the ball back towards the crowded area, and after Fink failed to clear sufficiently, the ball arrived at the feet of Giggs on the edge of the area. His right-footed snap-shot was weak and poorly struck, but it went straight to Sheringham, who swiped at the shot with his right foot, and nestled the ball in the bottom corner of the net. The goal was timed at 36 seconds into injury time.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-72) It looked as if, having been behind for most of the match, United had forced extra time.

> You have to feel this is their year. Is this their moment? Beckham, into Sheringham – _and Solskjær has won it!_ Manchester United have reached the promised land! Ole Solskjær! The two substitutes have scored the two goals in stoppage time and the treble looms large!

—Tyldesley on ITV's broadcast of Solskjær's injury time winner[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-The_Commentator's_Tale-71)

Less than 30 seconds after the subsequent kick-off, United forced another corner when Kuffour deflected Solskjær's cross over the Bayern goal line, but Schmeichel stayed in his penalty area this time, under instruction from Ferguson. Beckham again swung the corner in, finding the head of Sheringham, who nodded the ball down across the face of goal. Solskjær reacted fastest, stuck out a foot and poked the ball into the roof of the Bayern goal for United to take the lead with just 43 seconds of the three minutes of injury time to play. Solskjær celebrated by sliding on his knees, mimicking Basler's earlier celebration, before quickly being mobbed by the United players, substitutes and coaching staff.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-73) Schmeichel, in his own penalty area, cartwheeled with glee.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-74)

The game restarted, but many Bayern players were overwhelmed with despair, virtually unable to continue and needed the assistance of referee Collina to drag themselves off the ground.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-75) They were stunned to have lost a game they had thought won just minutes before; several celebratory flares had already been ignited by the Bayern fans moments before United equalised, and ribbons in the club's colours had already been secured to the trophy in preparation for the presentation ceremony.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-76) United held onto their lead to record their second European Cup title,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-77) and at the final whistle, referee Collina described the cheers from the fans as being like a "lion's roar".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-78) Kuffour broke down in tears after the game, beating the floor in despair, and Jancker collapsed in anguish.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-79) Matthäus had captained Bayern in the [1987 European Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final") and lost in similar circumstances to two late Porto goals. He had been substituted with 10 minutes remaining, with victory seemingly assured.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-mirror-80)

The **1999 UEFA Champions League final** was an [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") match between [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") of England and [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") of Germany, played at [Camp Nou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou") in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Spain, on 26 May 1999, to determine the winner of the [1998–99 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_UEFA_Champions_League "1998–99 UEFA Champions League"). [Injury time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football#Duration_and_tie-breaking_methods "Association football") goals from Manchester United's [Teddy Sheringham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Sheringham "Teddy Sheringham") and [Ole Gunnar Solskjær](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ole_Gunnar_Solskj%C3%A6r "Ole Gunnar Solskjær") cancelled out [Mario Basler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Basler "Mario Basler")'s early goal for Bayern to give Manchester United a 2–1 win and their first European Cup title since [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_European_Cup_final "1968 European Cup final"), their second overall. Referee Pierluigi Collina has cited this match as one of the most memorable of his career, and described the noise from the crowd at the end of the game as being like a "lion's roar".

The two sides had played each other earlier in the competition, having both been drawn in Group D in the group stage; Bayern won the group, while Manchester United qualified for the knockout phase as one of the two best runners-up across all six groups. After beating [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan") in the quarter-finals, Manchester United beat another Italian side, [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC"), in the semis to reach the final; meanwhile, Bayern beat fellow Germans [1. FC Kaiserslautern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Kaiserslautern "1. FC Kaiserslautern") in the quarter-finals, before overcoming Ukrainian side [Dynamo Kyiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Dynamo_Kyiv "FC Dynamo Kyiv") in the semis. The victory completed a [treble-winning season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_Manchester_United_F.C._season "1998–99 Manchester United F.C. season") for Manchester United, having already secured the [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_FA_Premier_League "1998–99 FA Premier League") and [FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_FA_Cup "1998–99 FA Cup") titles in the preceding 10 days. Bayern were also playing for a treble, having won the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_Bundesliga "1998–99 Bundesliga") and reached the [DFB-Pokal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_DFB-Pokal "1998–99 DFB-Pokal") final, although they went on to lose [that match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_DFB-Pokal_Final "1999 DFB-Pokal Final") as well to [Werder Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SV_Werder_Bremen "SV Werder Bremen") on penalties. It has been widely regarded as one of the greatest finals in the history of the tournament.

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C.") and [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") had only met twice in competitive matches before the final, both meetings coming earlier in the 1998–99 season and both finished as draws.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-head_to_head-2) Manchester United's only other German opponents in their history were [Borussia Dortmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borussia_Dortmund "Borussia Dortmund"), against whom they had an overall winning record, with three wins, two defeats and a draw in their six matches, including a 10–1 aggregate win in the second round of the [1964–65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964%E2%80%9365_Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup "1964–65 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup") and a 2–0 aggregate defeat in the [1996–97 UEFA Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996%E2%80%9397_UEFA_Champions_League "1996–97 UEFA Champions League") semi-finals.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-3) Bayern Munich had an equally narrow advantage in their 22 matches against English opposition, with seven wins, nine draws and six defeats, including a win over [Leeds United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_United_F.C. "Leeds United F.C.") in the [1975 European Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_European_Cup_final "1975 European Cup final") and a defeat to [Aston Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aston_Villa_F.C. "Aston Villa F.C.") in the [1982 final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_European_Cup_final "1982 European Cup final").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-4)

Including the victory over Leeds in 1975, Bayern Munich had won the European Cup on three occasions going into the 1999 final. With three victories in a row from [1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_European_Cup_final "1974 European Cup final") to [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_European_Cup_final "1976 European Cup final"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-5) they became only the third team to achieve such a feat after [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF") ([1956](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_European_Cup_final "1956 European Cup final") to [1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960_European_Cup_final "1960 European Cup final"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-6) and [Ajax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFC_Ajax "AFC Ajax") ([1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_European_Cup_final "1971 European Cup final") to [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_European_Cup_final "1973 European Cup final")).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-7) They had also finished as runners-up twice: in 1982 against Aston Villa[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-8) and [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_European_Cup_final "1987 European Cup final") against [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Porto "FC Porto").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-9) Although Bayern had been waiting 23 years for a European Cup title, Manchester United had had to wait even longer, as their only victory had come in [1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_European_Cup_final "1968 European Cup final") against [Benfica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S.L._Benfica "S.L. Benfica") at Wembley in extra time.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-10) Their manager then was [Matt Busby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Busby "Matt Busby"), who had been seriously injured 10 years earlier in the [Munich air disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_air_disaster "Munich air disaster"), which killed eight of his players on the way back from a European Cup tie in Belgrade, before rebuilding the team to become European Cup winners. Busby died in 1994; the day of the 1999 Champions League final would have been his 90th birthday.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-treble_joy-11)

Although it was the second Champions League season to feature clubs that had not won their national leagues the year before, Manchester United and Bayern Munich were the first such clubs to reach the final of the competition.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):354 Nevertheless, both went into the match as champions, having won their domestic leagues in 1998–99; Bayern Munich claimed the [Bundesliga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesliga "Bundesliga") title with a 1–1 draw against [Hertha BSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertha_BSC "Hertha BSC") on 9 May with three games to go, while Manchester United left it until the last day of the season (16 May), when they came back from 1–0 down against [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C.") to win 2–1 and beat [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_F.C. "Arsenal F.C.") to the title by a point.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-13) Both teams were also playing for the [treble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treble_(association_football) "Treble (association football)"); in addition to their league win, Manchester United had beaten [Newcastle United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_United_F.C. "Newcastle United F.C.") in the [1999 FA Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FA_Cup_Final "1999 FA Cup Final") on 22 May to claim the [Double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_(association_football) "Double (association football)"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-14) while Bayern were due to play [Werder Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SV_Werder_Bremen "SV Werder Bremen") in the [1999 DFB-Pokal Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998%E2%80%9399_DFB-Pokal "1998–99 DFB-Pokal") on 12 June.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-sky_treble-15)

### Qualifying round

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Qualifying round")]

Since neither Manchester United nor Bayern Munich had won their respective leagues in 1997–98, both sides faced a qualifier to enter the 1998–99 Champions League. Manchester United were drawn against Polish champions [ŁKS Łódź](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81KS_%C5%81%C3%B3d%C5%BA "ŁKS Łódź") and won 2–0 on aggregate, goals from [Ryan Giggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Giggs "Ryan Giggs") and [Andy Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Cole "Andy Cole") in the first leg at [Old Trafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Trafford "Old Trafford") giving them the victory.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-17) Bayern Munich had an easier time against Yugoslavian champions [Obilić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK_Obili%C4%87 "FK Obilić"), winning 4–0 in the first leg at the [Olympiastadion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiastadion_(Munich) "Olympiastadion (Munich)") with goals from [Stefan Effenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Effenberg "Stefan Effenberg"), [Giovane Élber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovane_%C3%89lber "Giovane Élber"), [Alexander Zickler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Zickler "Alexander Zickler") and [Thorsten Fink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorsten_Fink "Thorsten Fink"), all scored in the space of 17 second-half minutes.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-18) In the second leg, played at [Partizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FK_Partizan "FK Partizan")'s ground in Belgrade, an 88th-minute goal from [Lothar Matthäus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothar_Matth%C3%A4us "Lothar Matthäus") rescued a 1–1 draw to give Bayern a 5–1 win on aggregate.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-19)

### Group stage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Group stage")]

In the draw for the group stage, Bayern Munich were placed in Pot 2 and Manchester United in Pot 3 as Germany was higher than England in the UEFA association club coefficient rankings. They were drawn together in Group D, along with Spanish champions [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") and Danish champions [Brøndby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%B8ndby_IF "Brøndby IF"), in what became known as the "group of death".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-20) United and Bayern found themselves bottom of the group after the first round of matches, in which Bayern lost 2–1 away to Brøndby after surrendering a 1–0 lead in the last three minutes;[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-21) United, meanwhile, played out a 3–3 draw at home to Barcelona after twice giving up the lead.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-22) The first group stage meeting between United and Bayern took place at the Olympiastadion on matchday 2 and finished in a 2–2 draw; Élber opened the scoring for Bayern before goals from [Dwight Yorke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Yorke "Dwight Yorke") and [Paul Scholes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Scholes "Paul Scholes") gave United the lead, only for a [Teddy Sheringham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Sheringham "Teddy Sheringham") own goal – brought about by an error by [Peter Schmeichel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Schmeichel "Peter Schmeichel") – to level the scores in the 89th minute.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-23)

Matchdays 3 and 4 saw double-headers, with Manchester United taking on Brøndby and Bayern Munich playing Barcelona. Manchester United beat Brøndby 6–2 in their first match at [Parken Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parken_Stadium "Parken Stadium") in Copenhagen,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-24) then 5–0 at Old Trafford two weeks later.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-25) Bayern also recorded a pair of victories over Barcelona, winning 1–0 at the Olympiastadion[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-26) and 2–1 at the Camp Nou.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-27) On matchday 5, United played their second match against Barcelona – their first trip of the season to the Camp Nou – and again the two sides played out a 3–3 draw.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-28) With Bayern beating Brøndby 2–0 at home, the German side moved onto 10 points and took top spot in the group going into the final round of matches, one point ahead of United.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-29) Qualification for the quarter-finals was only guaranteed for the group winners,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-30) meaning that both United and Bayern had to play for victory in their final match against each other at Old Trafford. United took the lead just before half-time through a [Roy Keane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Keane "Roy Keane") strike from just outside the penalty area; however, [Hasan Salihamidžić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasan_Salihamid%C5%BEi%C4%87 "Hasan Salihamidžić") equalised for Bayern in the 55th minute and the game finished as a 1–1 draw. The result meant that Bayern finished as group winners, but United's 10 points from their six matches was enough to see them go through as one of the two group runners-up with the best record.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-33)

### Knockout stage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Knockout stage")]

In the quarter-finals, Bayern Munich were drawn against Group F winners and fellow German side [1. FC Kaiserslautern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1._FC_Kaiserslautern "1. FC Kaiserslautern"), while Manchester United were paired with Group C winners [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan"). Two Yorke goals gave United a 2–0 win in their first leg at Old Trafford,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-34) while Bayern beat Kaiserslautern by the same scoreline at the Olympiastadion through goals from Élber and Effenberg.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-35) In the second leg, [Nicola Ventola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Ventola "Nicola Ventola") pulled a goal back for Inter, but Paul Scholes secured United's passage to the semi-finals with a late away goal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-36) Meanwhile, Bayern won convincingly at Kaiserslautern, as goals from Effenberg, [Carsten Jancker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carsten_Jancker "Carsten Jancker"), [Mario Basler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Basler "Mario Basler") and an own goal from [Uwe Rösler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uwe_R%C3%B6sler "Uwe Rösler") gave them a 4–0 win, 6–0 on aggregate.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-37)

United again came up against Italian opposition in the semi-finals, facing [Juventus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC "Juventus FC"), who had beaten Greek side [Olympiacos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiacos_F.C. "Olympiacos F.C.") in the quarters, and Bayern were drawn against Ukrainian side [Dynamo Kyiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Dynamo_Kyiv "FC Dynamo Kyiv"), who beat reigning champions Real Madrid to reach the semis. Both first legs finished as draws; Giggs scored in injury time to secure a 1–1 home draw for Manchester United after [Antonio Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Conte "Antonio Conte") had put Juventus ahead midway through the first half,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-38) while Bayern also had to come from behind to draw 3–3 in Kyiv.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-39) A single goal from Basler proved the difference between Bayern and Dynamo in the second leg, giving the Germans a 4–3 aggregate win.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-40) Manchester United fell behind early in the [second leg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juventus_FC_2%E2%80%933_Manchester_United_F.C. "Juventus FC 2–3 Manchester United F.C.") in Turin, as [Filippo Inzaghi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filippo_Inzaghi "Filippo Inzaghi") scored twice in the first 11 minutes. Goals from Keane and Yorke before half-time levelled the tie but gave United the advantage on away goals, before Cole secured victory with the winning goal seven minutes from the end of the match.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-41)

## Pre-match

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Pre-match")]

### Venue and ticketing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Venue and ticketing")]

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Camp_Nou_aerial_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Camp_Nou_aerial_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Camp_Nou_aerial_(cropped).jpg)

The capacity of the [Camp Nou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou") stadium was reduced from over 100,000 to 92,000 for the final.

The [Camp Nou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Nou "Camp Nou") stadium in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Spain, was selected as the venue for the final at a meeting of the UEFA Executive Committee in Lisbon, Portugal, on 6 October 1998.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-42) The selection process had begun more than four months earlier, in May 1998, when FC Barcelona submitted the Camp Nou as a contender to host the match in recognition of the club's centenary year.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-43) The other venues in contention to host the match were London's [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)") and Marseille's [Stade Vélodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_V%C3%A9lodrome "Stade Vélodrome"), but the Camp Nou was considered by UEFA's Stadiums Commission to be the favourite for its superior security, comfort and capacity.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-44) The Camp Nou had hosted one previous European Cup final: Italian club [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Milan "AC Milan")'s 4–0 victory over [Steaua București](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FCSB "FCSB") of Romania in [1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_European_Cup_final "1989 European Cup final"). It had also hosted two [Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup "UEFA Cup Winners' Cup") finals, in [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final "1972 European Cup Winners' Cup Final") and [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup_Final "1982 European Cup Winners' Cup Final"); the latter was won on home turf by Barcelona.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-45)

The Camp Nou was constructed over three years from 1954 to 1957 as a replacement for Barcelona's previous home, the nearby [Camp de Les Corts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_de_Les_Corts "Camp de Les Corts").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-camp_nou_history-46) The original capacity of the Camp Nou was just over 93,000,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-camp_nou_history-46) but its first major European final, the 1972 Cup Winners' Cup Final, was attended by just 35,000 spectators.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-47) 1982 was the stadium's busiest year to date, hosting not only the 1982 Cup Winners' Cup Final, but also five matches at the [FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_FIFA_World_Cup "1982 FIFA World Cup"), including the opening match, all three matches in Group A of the second group stage and the semi-final between [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland_national_football_team "Poland national football team") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_national_football_team "Italy national football team"). Subsequent renovations meant that by 1999, the stadium's capacity had reached 115,000.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-camp_nou_history-46)

Due to UEFA regulations regarding standing at football matches, the Camp Nou's terraced sections were closed for the 1999 Champions League final, reducing the capacity to approximately 92,000. Of these, around two-thirds were reserved for the two finalist clubs (approximately 30,000 tickets each). The remaining third was divided between fans of FC Barcelona (around 7,500 tickets), UEFA, and competition sponsors.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):339 After an initial announcement that the clubs would only receive 25,000 tickets each, the [Independent Manchester United Supporters Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Manchester_United_Supporters_Association "Independent Manchester United Supporters Association") (IMUSA) called that figure "ridiculous", claiming it would push black market prices to "astronomical levels"; the group's spokesman, Lee Hodgkiss, suggested a figure closer to 50,000 would be more appropriate, given the stadium's usual capacity of around 115,000.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-48) Despite the club receiving only 30,000 tickets, it was estimated that up to 100,000 Manchester United fans travelled to Barcelona for the final, paying around £300 for flights and around £1,000 for match tickets.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):346 Many were able to buy tickets from touts, who had paid up to £400 to buy from Barcelona fans who had bought through their club for the equivalent of £28.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):339–340

As well as reducing the capacity of the stadium, UEFA also mandated that the Camp Nou pitch be narrowed by 4 metres (13 ft) from 72 metres (236 ft) to 68 metres (223 ft), to match UEFA's 'standard' pitch size.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):327

### Match officials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Match officials")]

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Pierluigi_Collina_2010.jpg/250px-Pierluigi_Collina_2010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pierluigi_Collina_2010.jpg)

Pierluigi Collina was the referee for the match.

The match referee was Pierluigi Collina of the [Italian Football Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Football_Federation "Italian Football Federation"). Collina was promoted to the FIFA International Referees list in 1995, and took charge of his first UEFA Cup matches in the [1995–96 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995%E2%80%9396_UEFA_Cup "1995–96 UEFA Cup"). He had only refereed eight Champions League matches before the 1999 final, three of which came in the group stage earlier in the season, including the match between Barcelona and Bayern Munich at the Camp Nou on 4 November 1998; however, he had also taken charge of four matches at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_tournament "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament"), including the final between [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria_national_under-23_football_team "Nigeria national under-23 football team") and [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_under-23_football_team "Argentina national under-23 football team"), and two group stage matches at the [1998 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_FIFA_World_Cup "1998 FIFA World Cup").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-49) Collina was supported by fellow Italian officials Gennaro Mazzei and [Claudio Puglisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Puglisi?action=edit&redlink=1 "Claudio Puglisi (page does not exist)") as assistant referees, and fourth official Fiorenzo Treossi.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-officials-50)

### Match ball

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Match ball")]

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Nike_NK_800_Geo_1999_Champions_League_Final.JPG/250px-Nike_NK_800_Geo_1999_Champions_League_Final.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nike_NK_800_Geo_1999_Champions_League_Final.JPG)

One of the [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") NK 800 Geo balls used for the final

The match ball for the final was the Nike NK 800 Geo, a white ball with a standard 32-panel design. It featured a large "[swoosh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swoosh "Swoosh")" across two adjacent hexagonal panels with the Champions League logo on a pentagonal panel above, and a pattern of five-pointed stars similar to those used in the UEFA Champions League logo over the entire surface of the ball.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-51)

### Kits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Kits")]

As both Manchester United and Bayern Munich's primary kits featured significant amounts of red, UEFA regulations about kit clashes would normally have required both teams to wear their change kits. However, the two clubs felt it would have been a shame for neither to wear their traditional colours, and they agreed to toss a coin to see who would have first choice. Manchester United won the toss and therefore wore their usual European colours of red shirts, white shorts and white socks, while Bayern wore silver shirts, shorts and socks, all with maroon trim.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-Ferris-12):360

### Opening ceremony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Opening ceremony")]

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_opening_ceremony.jpg/250px-1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_opening_ceremony.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1999_UEFA_Champions_League_Final_opening_ceremony.jpg)

The opening ceremony featured inflatable versions of recognisable Barcelona landmarks.

Before kick-off, opera singer [Montserrat Caballé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montserrat_Caball%C3%A9 "Montserrat Caballé") – moving around the field on the back of a golf cart[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-52) – performed a live version of "[Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_(Freddie_Mercury_and_Montserrat_Caball%C3%A9_song) "Barcelona (Freddie Mercury and Montserrat Caballé song)")", a song she recorded with the late [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)") lead singer [Freddie Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Mercury "Freddie Mercury") in 1987, accompanied by a recording of Mercury on the stadium's electronic screen.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-53) The opening ceremony featured inflatable versions of some of Barcelona's most recognisable landmarks,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-leith_132-54) as well as flag-bearers waving flags of the crests of the participating teams. Bayern Munich's fans, meanwhile, created a [tifo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tifo "Tifo") of the name of their team with thousands of coloured cards.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_UEFA_Champions_League_final#cite_note-leith_132-54)
